title: The Art of Computer Programming: Milwaukee to Stanford, and the Ten-Year Detour
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Milwaukee, born to the man with the press
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: A son is born in Milwaukee to Ervin Henry Knuth, who teaches bookkeeping at a business school and plays for his Lutheran church, and to Louise Marie Bohning. They name him Donald Ervin. There is a small printing press in the family's keeping, and the boy grows up around ink and the discipline of setting a line straight, a trade his father works at the edges of his teaching. Sixty years later the son will spend a decade rebuilding in software the craft that goes out of the world's print shops while he watches.
suggested_refs: Milwaukee's Lutheran parish and business-school world of the 1930s, the family trade of type and ledgers

stops.name: Milwaukee, the Ziegler's Giant Bar contest
stops.date_confidence: eighth-grade year attested; for a January 1938 birth that is the 1951-52 school year; month not recorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: In his eighth-grade year a candy company runs a contest: how many words can be spelled from the letters in Ziegler's Giant Bar. The judges hold a list of roughly 2,500, and that list is the standard every entry is measured against. Knuth works at it with a dictionary open on the table, week after week, and turns in more than 4,500. He is thirteen or fourteen. The school receives a television set for it, and every one of his schoolmates receives a candy bar.
suggested_refs: The Ziegler Candy Company promotional contest of 1951-52 and its word lists
sources: American Scientist and ACM profiles of Knuth

stops.name: Milwaukee Lutheran High School, the highest average on record
stops.date_confidence: graduation year attested; month conventional for a June commencement
stops.campa: He graduates from Milwaukee Lutheran High School, out on Ninety-Seventh Street, with the highest grade point average the school has recorded. The subject on the paperwork is physics: a scholarship to Case Institute of Technology in Cleveland is waiting on that assumption. The other training is music, the church-organ music of his father's Lutheran world, and he keeps it up. Nothing in the record says he has yet touched a computer. The school honors him again in 1996.
suggested_refs: Milwaukee Lutheran High School at 97th and West Grantosa Drive, which honored him again in 1996

segments.name: Case, and the Machine in the Basement

stops.name: Case Institute of Technology, the physics scholarship
stops.date_confidence: term of entry attested; day conventional
stops.campa: Knuth arrives in Cleveland on a physics scholarship and finds the subject less hospitable than mathematics, and mathematics less absorbing than the IBM 650 the campus keeps in a room that hums. Case is a technical institute with an unusual policy: undergraduates are allowed near the machine. He reads its manual, decides the sample programs printed in it can be written better, and rewrites them. The physics does not last two years. He spends his nights with the 650, going back through code that already runs, looking for the version that reads more clearly.
suggested_refs: The IBM 650 installation at Case and its undergraduate access policy

stops.name: Case Institute of Technology, the Potrzebie System
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month taken from the issue in which it appeared
stops.campa: A freshman sells a parody to Mad magazine. The Potrzebie System of Weights and Measures takes as its fundamental unit of length the thickness of Mad issue 26, and derives from it a whole apparatus of units, conversions and tables, executed with more rigor than the joke requires. There are units for mass, for time, for temperature, for money, all of them named and all of them convertible into one another. It runs in issue 33, and it is the first thing Donald Knuth publishes.
suggested_refs: Mad magazine issue 33 (1957), 'The Potrzebie System of Weights and Measures'

stops.name: Case Institute of Technology, the basketball formula
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the geography lens carried 1957 in error, corrected here to 1958; month unrecorded
stops.campa: The basketball coach wants to know which of his players is actually contributing. Knuth, an undergraduate with access to the machine, writes a formula weighing each man's passes, rebounds and shots against what they cost the team, and feeds a season of statistics through the IBM 650. The coach uses it. He is twenty years old, and the story travels: Newsweek covers it, and CBS sends a camera to Cleveland to film an undergraduate feeding a basketball season into a computer.
suggested_refs: The 1958 Newsweek item and CBS Evening News segment on the Case basketball program

stops.name: Case Institute of Technology, two degrees on one day
stops.date_confidence: year attested; June commencement conventional
stops.campa: He leaves Case with a bachelor of science in mathematics and, by a special vote of the faculty, a master of science awarded the same day for the same undergraduate work. The faculty has no other instrument to mark what he has done. He is twenty-two, and by the time he leaves Cleveland he has a place in graduate mathematics at Caltech and a consulting contract already signed with a computer company in Pasadena. The graduate years are to be paid for by writing compilers. He goes west in the summer of 1960.
suggested_refs: The Case faculty vote awarding a master's degree for undergraduate work, 1960

segments.name: Pasadena: A Compiler, a Marriage, and a Book That Will Not Close

stops.name: Burroughs Corporation, Pasadena, the ALGOL compiler
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month inferred from the summer before graduate entry; the Pasadena office coordinates are a reconstruction
stops.campa: Burroughs pays him five thousand five hundred dollars to write an ALGOL compiler for the B205. It is more money than a graduate student in 1960 has any business seeing. The contract turns into eight years of part-time consulting, through the B220 and beyond, and it teaches him compilers from the inside: the passes, the symbol tables, the places where a language design makes the implementer's life impossible. When a publisher asks him two years later to write a book about compilers, he is not guessing.
suggested_refs: The Burroughs B205 ALGOL compiler, written under a $5,500 contract

stops.name: Caltech, graduate study under Marshall Hall
stops.date_confidence: year attested; September term conventional
stops.campa: He enters the mathematics department at Caltech to work under Marshall Hall Jr., in a field with no obvious relation to the machines he programs in the evenings. Projective planes and finite semifields are pure structure: objects that either exist for a given order or provably do not. He will finish the doctorate in three years. The days belong to finite geometry and the evenings to Burroughs, and he keeps both schedules for the length of the degree, without treating either one as the interruption.
suggested_refs: The Caltech mathematics department under Marshall Hall Jr., specialist in combinatorics and group theory

stops.name: Pasadena, marriage to Nancy Jill Carter
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in Knuth's own curriculum vitae; the ceremony venue is not established
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of June a Caltech graduate student marries Nancy Jill Carter. How they met the sources do not say; one careless account makes her a fellow student on the same campus, which nothing consulted here supports. The marriage runs alongside every volume, every rewrite, every decade-long detour that follows. Of Nancy Jill Carter herself the reachable record holds a name and a date in her husband's curriculum vitae, and nothing further at all.
suggested_refs: Knuth's curriculum vitae entry for 24 June 1961

stops.name: Addison-Wesley, Reading, the commission for one book
stops.date_confidence: January 1962 attested; whether Knuth was in Reading or corresponded by mail is not established
stops.campa: In January a publisher's editor asks the twenty-four-year-old to write a book about compilers. Knuth agrees, and before the day is out he has sketched twelve chapter titles. The scope has already slipped: chapter one is basic concepts, chapter two is information structures, and the compiler itself has receded toward the back of the book. He signs on for one volume. Sixty years later he is still working on it, and the twelve chapters have become a projected seven books of which four are in print.
suggested_refs: The original twelve-chapter outline of January 1962, preserved in Knuth's account of the project

stops.name: Caltech, the doctorate and the assistant professorship
stops.date_confidence: June 1963 attested for the degree; the faculty appointment follows in the same year
stops.campa: The thesis is called Finite Semifields and Projective Planes: an inquiry into which finite geometries can exist at all. Hall signs it, Caltech grants the doctorate, and the department keeps its own graduate on as assistant professor of mathematics. He is twenty-five, teaching pure mathematics, consulting on compilers across town, and writing at night a book that has already outgrown its contract. None of this is called computer science at Caltech, because at Caltech in 1963 there is no such department.
suggested_refs: Knuth, 'Finite Semifields and Projective Planes' (Caltech PhD thesis, 1963)

stops.name: Caltech, three thousand pages in longhand
stops.date_confidence: June 1965 attested; the chronology lens carried this loosely as 'by 1966' and is corrected here
stops.campa: In June he finishes the first complete draft: roughly three thousand pages in longhand, written to become a single book. He sends it east. Addison-Wesley works out what three thousand handwritten pages become in type and reports back that this is not a book, it is a shelf. Nothing is cut. The manuscript is broken into volumes instead, and the breaking is a publisher's decision about binding rather than an author's decision about scope. Knuth is twenty-seven.
suggested_refs: The 3,000-page holograph draft of June 1965

stops.name: Caltech, seven volumes and an associate professorship
stops.date_confidence: the restructuring falls in 1965-66; the promotion is dated 1966; month unrecorded
stops.campa: The plan settles at seven volumes: fundamental algorithms, seminumerical algorithms, sorting and searching, combinatorial algorithms, and three further out toward languages and compilers. Caltech promotes him to associate professor. He is twenty-eight. Each algorithm in the seven volumes is to be stated exactly, analyzed for what it costs, and proved correct. No survey of any field has been attempted on those terms, and the field itself does not yet have a name everyone agrees on.
suggested_refs: Addison-Wesley's seven-volume restructuring of The Art of Computer Programming

segments.name: Princeton and the Move to Stanford

stops.name: Addison-Wesley, Reading, Volume 1 set in hot metal
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: Fundamental Algorithms appears from Addison-Wesley in Reading, Massachusetts, set in Monotype by a printer working in hot metal: molten lead cast into type, line by line, by a machine and a man who both know the trade. The mathematics on the page is beautiful, and Knuth knows exactly how beautiful, having spent six years looking at proofs of it. He will not see typography of this quality from his publisher again. Nine years later that fact will cost him a decade.
suggested_refs: The Monotype hot-metal setting of the 1968 first edition of Volume 1

stops.name: Institute for Defense Analyses, Princeton, the classified year
stops.date_confidence: 1968-1969 per Knuth's CV; the geography lens carried 1967-1969 in error; the coordinates are the atlas pin for the Institute for Advanced Study grounds, adjacent to which the Communications Research Division sat
stops.campa: For a year Knuth works as a staff mathematician at the Institute for Defense Analyses, in the Communications Research Division on the Princeton grounds, doing cryptography in support of the National Security Agency. The work is classified and stays that way; what he did there across 1968 and 1969 is not known. He is a few hundred yards from the Institute for Advanced Study, where John von Neumann wrote the first substantial program for a stored-program machine two decades earlier. Knuth reconstructs that program instruction by instruction and publishes it in 1970.
suggested_refs: Knuth, 'Von Neumann's First Computer Program', Computing Surveys (1970)

stops.name: Stanford, the chair in computer science
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: Knuth's CV and MacTutor date the appointment 1968, Wikipedia dates it 1969; dated here to arrival on campus after the Princeton year
stops.campa: He resigns Caltech and Burroughs both and takes a professorship in computer science at Stanford, in a department founded four years earlier by George Forsythe on the argument that programming is a subject and not a service. He arrives as a mathematician who writes about programs and settles in as the man who defines what analyzing a program means. He stays for the rest of his life. His own curriculum vitae dates the appointment to 1968 and other accounts to 1969, the year turning on whether the Princeton contract or the Stanford campus is counted.
suggested_refs: The Stanford Computer Science Department, founded 1965 under George Forsythe

stops.name: Addison-Wesley, Reading, Volume 2
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month unrecorded, placed after the Stanford arrival
stops.campa: Seminumerical Algorithms is published: random numbers and arithmetic, the two subjects in which a computer's answers are least like a mathematician's. The volume carries his statistical tests for randomness and his treatment of floating point as a thing with error rather than a thing with results. Von Neumann's middle-square method for generating random digits is taken apart in it with data, and found wanting. He is writing the third volume at the same time, in a Stanford office he has occupied for a matter of months.
suggested_refs: The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 2, chapter 3, on random numbers

stops.name: Stanford, the first Grace Murray Hopper Award
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: The Association for Computing Machinery establishes an award for young computer professionals, names it for Grace Murray Hopper, and Knuth is the first person to receive it. The citation rests on Fundamental Algorithms, a book by a mathematician about a craft that most of the profession still learns at the machine rather than from a book. He receives it in the middle of drafting the third volume. He is thirty-three. Two volumes are in print, the third is in draft, and the fourth has not been begun.
suggested_refs: ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award, first conferral, 1971

stops.name: University of Oslo, Blindern, Surreal Numbers
stops.date_confidence: the sabbatical year 1972-73 is attested; the month of arrival is not recorded
stops.campa: On sabbatical at Blindern, with the third volume unfinished on the desk, Knuth reads John Conway's construction of the surreal numbers and cannot let it alone. He writes a novella. Two young people on a beach find a stone with two rules carved into it and derive an entire number system from first principles, arguing their way forward with nothing else to go on. It is published as Surreal Numbers, an experiment in teaching mathematics as discovery rather than as exposition. Then he goes back to sorting.
suggested_refs: Knuth, Surreal Numbers (Addison-Wesley, 1974), written at Oslo

stops.name: Addison-Wesley, Reading, Volume 3
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: Sorting and Searching is published, six hundred pages on the two operations a computer spends most of its life performing. The question it asks of a method is not whether the method works but what it costs, and the answer is required in a form that holds for every input size: how many comparisons, on average, in the worst case, asymptotically, with the constants named. Work on the fourth volume begins the same year. Volume 4A appears thirty-eight years later.
suggested_refs: The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 3, Sorting and Searching (1973)

stops.name: San Diego, the Turing Award lecture
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; the San Diego conference venue and the November date are a reconstruction, not verified in this pass
stops.campa: The Association for Computing Machinery gives Knuth the Turing Award, its highest honor, for the analysis of algorithms and the design of programming languages. The prize carries the name of Alan Turing, who defined the algorithm as a formal object two years before Knuth was born and long before there was a machine to run one on. The lecture Knuth delivers in reply is titled Computer Programming as an Art, and it argues that the discipline has an aesthetics as well as a set of metrics. The following year he is elected to the National Academy of Sciences.
stops.quote: The real problem is that programmers have spent far too much time worrying about efficiency in the wrong places and at the wrong times; premature optimization is the root of all evil (or at least most of it) in programming.
stops.quote_source: Donald Knuth, 'Computer Programming as an Art', Turing Award lecture, Communications of the ACM 17:12 (December 1974), p. 671
suggested_refs: Knuth, 'Computer Programming as an Art', CACM 17:12 (1974), pp. 667-673

stops.name: Stanford, the galley proofs of the second edition
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of March the proofs of the second edition arrive and Knuth opens them. The printer who set the first edition in hot metal is gone, and these pages have been produced photographically: the letterforms are thin, the mathematics sits wrong on the line, the book he spent six years writing looks cheap. He is told this is how books are made now. Within two months he decides that if the trade can no longer set mathematics properly he will write the program that does, and that it ought to take about a year.
suggested_refs: The 1977 galley proofs for the second edition of Volume 2, the proximate cause of TeX

stops.name: Stanford, the memo of 13 May
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He writes a memo. It describes a system for typesetting technical documents in which the author, not a compositor, specifies the page: fonts, boxes, glue between the boxes, line breaks chosen by minimizing a measure of badness across a whole paragraph instead of one line at a time. He calls it TeX, from the Greek root that gives both technology and text, and specifies that the final consonant is pronounced as in Bach. The memo is internal, dated the thirteenth of May, and circulated at Stanford.
suggested_refs: Knuth's internal Stanford memo of 13 May 1977 outlining TeX

stops.name: Stanford, Fletcher Jones Professor, and a name in Chinese
stops.date_confidence: both events dated to 1977; months unrecorded
stops.campa: Stanford names him Fletcher Jones Professor of Computer Science, a chair his own curriculum vitae records him holding until 1989. The same year the computer scientist Frances Yao gives him a Chinese name, Gao Dena, chosen to answer to the sound of his own and to mean something in its own right. He adopts it as his formal name in Chinese, and it goes on the Chinese editions of his books. The Art of Computer Programming stands at three volumes in print and one in draft. Work on it has stopped.
suggested_refs: The Chinese editions of TAOCP published under the name Gao Dena

stops.name: Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, TeX78
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded; the SAIL site coordinates are a reconstruction
stops.campa: In the foothills above the campus, in the building that houses the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, the first working TeX is written in the SAIL language for a PDP-10 running the WAITS operating system. It sets its first pages this year. The estimate of one year has already failed, and the system will be torn down and rebuilt from nothing before he is finished with it. He is also designing the typefaces, because there are none available that he considers adequate for mathematics.
suggested_refs: TeX78, written in SAIL for the PDP-10 under WAITS

stops.name: Stanford, Guy Steele's summer
stops.date_confidence: the summer of 1978 is attested; the exact month is conventional
stops.campa: Guy Steele spends the summer at Stanford in the room where TeX is being built. He carries the system back east with him, and that autumn he adapts its input and output routines to run under the Incompatible Timesharing System at MIT. It is the first port, made in the year the system first set a page, and Knuth neither charges for it nor objects to it. The routines Steele rewrites are the ones that touch the machine. The rest of TeX crosses the country unchanged.
suggested_refs: Guy Steele's 1978 adaptation of TeX for MIT's ITS

stops.name: Washington, the National Medal of Science
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; the White House venue and the month are conventional for the period, not separately confirmed
stops.campa: Jimmy Carter presents the National Medal of Science to a forty-one-year-old professor whose principal work is a book he has not finished and a program he has not stopped rewriting. The citation is for the analysis of algorithms. In the same period Knuth is privately using a system he calls DOC, after an idea of Pierre-Arnoul de Marneffe, which lets him keep a program and its explanation in a single file. Nothing about that is public yet, and he mentions it to almost no one.
suggested_refs: Pierre-Arnoul de Marneffe's 1973 proposals on program documentation, the precursor to DOC and WEB

stops.name: Stanford, WEB
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: Knuth releases WEB. A program is written once, as prose with the code embedded in it in whatever order explains it best, and then processed twice. One tool, tangle, extracts compilable Pascal in the order the machine requires. The other, weave, produces a TeX document in the order a reader requires, indexed and cross-referenced throughout. He builds WEB in order to write TeX in it, and the source of the typesetting system is then printed and bound between covers, its explanation running alongside the code it explains.
stops.quote: The main idea is to treat a program as a piece of literature, addressed to human beings rather than to a computer.
suggested_refs: The WEB system: tangle, weave, and the published source of TeX

stops.name: Stanford, TeX82 written again from nothing
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: He throws the whole system away and writes it a second time, in WEB, so that the program and its explanation are one document. TeX82 adopts Frank Liang's hyphenation algorithm, which learns its patterns from a dictionary instead of following rules. It abandons floating-point arithmetic entirely in favor of fixed point, so that identical input produces byte-identical output on every machine that will ever run it. A document set in TeX in 1982 sets the same way now.
stops.quote: Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it.
stops.quote_source: Donald Knuth, memo to Peter van Emde Boas (1977), reproduced on Knuth's Stanford FAQ page
suggested_refs: Frank Liang's 1983 Stanford dissertation on hyphenation by pattern matching

stops.name: Addison-Wesley, Reading, The TeXbook
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: Addison-Wesley publishes The TeXbook, the manual for the system, written in TeX and set by it. The book is layered: a reader can follow the main track and stop there, or take the dangerous-bend signs into material Knuth marks as harder than the rest. It is a manual with jokes in it, exercises, and answers to the exercises. Whatever else TeX is, it is now documented to a standard that commercial software of the period does not attempt. The companion volumes for METAFONT follow the same design two years later.
suggested_refs: The TeXbook (Addison-Wesley, 1984), volume A of Computers and Typesetting

stops.name: Stanford, the paper that names the practice
stops.date_confidence: the paper appears in volume 27, number 2 of the journal for 1984; the month is taken from that issue
stops.campa: The paper appears in The Computer Journal and gives the practice its name. Knuth's argument inverts the usual order of duty: a program's first audience is the human being reading it, and its executability is a secondary property that a tool can extract. Documentation is not a layer applied once the code works. The code is a byproduct of an essay about a problem. The systems actually written this way stay few enough to list by name. The idea is widely admired and narrowly adopted.
stops.quote: Instead of imagining that our main task is to instruct a computer what to do, let us concentrate rather on explaining to human beings what we want a computer to do.
stops.quote_source: Donald Knuth, 'Literate Programming', The Computer Journal 27:2 (1984), p. 97
suggested_refs: Knuth, 'Literate Programming', The Computer Journal 27:2 (1984), pp. 97-111

stops.name: SRI International, Menlo Park, LaTeX
stops.date_confidence: version 2.06a is dated September 1984; development runs from the early 1980s and the first manual follows in 1986
stops.campa: At SRI International in Menlo Park, twenty miles up the peninsula, Leslie Lamport has been writing TeX macros for his own papers and concludes that with a little more effort they could serve anyone. LaTeX is that effort: a layer of markup in which an author declares a section, a theorem, a bibliography, and lets the machinery underneath decide how those things look. Version 2.06a is released in September. LaTeX has no typesetting engine of its own and never acquires one; every LaTeX document ever compiled is compiled by running Knuth's program.
stops.quote: TeX is usually pronounced tech, making lah-tech, lah-tech, and lay-tech the logical choices; but language is not always logical, so lay-tecks is also possible.
stops.quote_source: Leslie Lamport, LaTeX: A Document Preparation System, as quoted in Wikipedia's 'LaTeX' article
suggested_refs: Lamport, LaTeX: A Document Preparation System (Addison-Wesley, 1986)

stops.name: Stanford, the source published as a book
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: Knuth publishes the source. TeX: The Program is the complete WEB listing of the typesetting system, some twenty thousand lines with their explanation woven through them, printed and bound as a volume of Computers and Typesetting. The METAFONTbook documents the companion system, in which a letterform is not a drawing but a program: a pen of a stated shape dragged along curves defined by parameters, so that a whole family of type can be generated by varying numbers.
stops.quote: Literate programming is a methodology that combines a programming language with a documentation language, thereby making programs more robust, more portable, more easily maintained, and arguably more fun to write than programs that are written only in a high-level language.
suggested_refs: Computers and Typesetting, volumes B through E, including TeX: The Program and The METAFONTbook

stops.name: Stanford, Concrete Mathematics
stops.date_confidence: 1989 per Knuth's CV; the chronology lens carried 1988 in error; month unrecorded
stops.campa: With Ronald Graham and Oren Patashnik, Knuth publishes Concrete Mathematics, grown out of a Stanford course invented to give computer science students the mathematics that Volume 1 assumes and no curriculum supplies. The book covers sums, recurrences and generating functions, and it standardizes the floor and ceiling notation. The margins carry graffiti written by the students who sat the course. It appears twenty-one years after the volume whose readers it is meant to prepare.
suggested_refs: Graham, Knuth and Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics (Addison-Wesley, 1989)

stops.name: Stanford, the end of email
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Knuth himself
stops.campa: On the first of January he gives up electronic mail, after fifteen years of having an address and being among the earliest academics anywhere to have one. Correspondence goes to a secretary and reaches him on paper, in batches, a few times a year. He keeps one channel open: readers who find errors in his books may still write, and those letters he answers himself. He built a good deal of the machinery he is walking away from. What he wants back is the uninterrupted week.
stops.quote: I have been a happy man ever since January 1, 1990, when I no longer had an email address.
suggested_refs: Knuth's 'Knuth versus Email' page, his own statement of the policy

stops.name: Stanford, version 3.0 and a chair named for a book
stops.date_confidence: the release is dated to the day; the change of title is dated to the year only
stops.campa: TeX reaches version 3.0 in March, with eight-bit input so that the world's accented and non-Latin alphabets can be set in it, and Knuth declares the system finished. Stanford, the same year, retitles him Professor of The Art of Computer Programming. From here versions are numbered by adding one digit at a time, 3.1, then 3.14, then 3.141, so that the number converges on pi. It becomes pi, he says, on the day he dies, and whatever bugs are left in it at that moment are to be considered features.
stops.quote: In fact, my main conclusion after spending ten years of my life working on the TEX project is that software is hard.
stops.quote_source: Donald Knuth, Notices of the American Mathematical Society (2002), as quoted on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The TeX version-numbering scheme converging on pi, and METAFONT's on e

stops.name: Stanford, emeritus at fifty-five
stops.date_confidence: retirement from teaching dated 1992, emeritus status 1993; months unrecorded
stops.campa: He stops teaching. In 1992 he takes early retirement from the classroom, and the Center for the Study of Language and Information publishes his collected papers on literate programming; the following year he becomes professor emeritus, keeping an office on a campus he does not leave. Four volumes are still to be written and one of them has not been begun, against a finite number of working years in which to write them. He is fifty-five, and he keeps the office.
stops.quote: What I do takes long hours of studying and uninterruptible concentration.
suggested_refs: Knuth, Literate Programming (CSLI, 1992)

stops.name: Kyoto, the Inamori Foundation's prize
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Knuth's CV, which also records his commemorative lecture in Kyoto; the November date follows the prize's usual calendar
stops.campa: The Inamori Foundation brings him to Kyoto for its prize in advanced technology, and he gives the commemorative lecture there. The award is one of the few that treats a body of work whole rather than a single discovery: the volumes, the typesetting system, the fonts, the argument that programs are literature. He is fifty-eight. The fourth volume of The Art of Computer Programming, begun in 1973, is still unpublished, and the fascicles of it that exist circulate as drafts among readers paid in imaginary currency to find its mistakes. He goes home to it.
suggested_refs: The 1996 Kyoto Prize commemorative lecture at the Kyoto International Conference Center

stops.name: Stanford, the Bank of San Serriffe
stops.date_confidence: the change of instrument is dated to 2008; month unrecorded
stops.campa: For decades Knuth has paid a finder's fee to any reader who catches an error in one of his books: two dollars and fifty-six cents for a genuine mistake, thirty-two cents for a suggestion worth taking. Many of the checks are never cashed. They are framed. In 2008, after check fraud makes the practice unsafe, he replaces them with certificates of deposit drawn on the Bank of San Serriffe, an institution that does not exist, in a country invented by a newspaper for the first of April.
suggested_refs: Knuth's errata policy pages and the certificates of the Bank of San Serriffe

stops.name: Stanford, Volume 4A after thirty-eight years
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: Combinatorial Algorithms, Part 1 is published, thirty-eight years after work on the fourth volume began. Its subject is generation: producing every tuple, permutation, combination and tree in a stated order and without repetition, which takes more pages than sorting and searching did, and a great many more years. Knuth is seventy-three. The material came out first in fascicles, drafts mailed to readers for correction and bound only once the corrections were in.
suggested_refs: The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 4A (2011), and the fascicle series preceding it

stops.name: Oxford, the Wolfson Building
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is recorded as running until 2017; its start date and the frequency of his visits are not established
stops.campa: For years he holds a visiting professorship at Oxford, in the Wolfson Building that houses the Department of Computer Science, and crosses the Atlantic to lecture there; the appointment runs until 2017. He is by then close to eighty, emeritus in a subject he helped to name, still lecturing in a foreign university out of an unfinished book. Oxford's own computing laboratory grew from the same postwar decade that produced the machines his first volume was written to describe, and by the time he lectures in it those machines survive only in his tables. How often he actually came the record does not say.

stops.name: Stanford, Volume 4B and the satisfiability problem
stops.date_confidence: September 2022 attested; one lens carried October in error
stops.campa: Combinatorial Algorithms, Part 2 appears in September, more than sixty years after twelve chapter titles were sketched in a publisher's meeting in January 1962. Its subject is satisfiability, the problem of deciding whether a set of logical constraints can be met at all, which has become in the interval a central practical problem of the field and did not exist as such when the outline was drawn. Knuth is eighty-four. Three of the seven volumes remain unwritten.

stops.name: Stanford, the house built around an organ
stops.date_confidence: ongoing; the residence coordinates are an approximation of the Stanford neighborhood, not a verified address
stops.campa: He lives near the campus in a house built around a music room, and the music room was built around a pipe organ of sixteen ranks that he plays himself. He composes for it. The music has run alongside the mathematics since Milwaukee, and neither of them has displaced the other. Visitors describe the workshop and the organ loft as one activity rather than two. Asked about the book, he has said for years that he does not expect to finish it, and the fascicles go out anyway and the errata come back. He is eighty-five. In the evenings he plays.
stops.quote: The important thing to me ... is not the destination, but the journey.
stops.quote_source: Knuth quoted in a Physics Today review of Things a Computer Scientist Rarely Talks About, reproduced on his Stanford page
